Once upon a time,

there was a world-famous orchestra conductor. People came from all over just to watch him lead the orchestra. As he waved his baton, the music seemed to come to life, enchanting the audience. He was also very humble, never wanting more than a modest stipend to cover his expenses and was very kind to anyone he met. Of course, he had a team of lawyers and publicists making money hand-over-fist on him due to his fame, but he was simply happy to lead the orchestra and nothing else.

One fateful day, during a typical performance, the maestro made a mistake. He forgot to cue the flute section. Of course, these were professionals, and the flutes came in at the right time anyway, but he knew in his mind that he had made a mistake. All these adoring fans came to see perfection, and he had let them all down. So after the concert he announced to his team of lawyers and publicists that he was done with public performances forever.

With a great sputtering and gnashing of teeth, his team insisted that nobody had noticed the mistake - it would be fine, nobody would notice. Besides, they had quite the cash cow going and they didn't want it to stop. So after hours of cajoling and strongly worded recommendations, the maestro agreed to go on stage again the next night.

The following night, in front of a packed house, he walked onto the stage, tapped his baton, and then pulled out a pistol and shot the first violinist.

Of course, he was immediately arrested. He was booked, taken to jail and put on trial. The jury found him guilty, and due to the graphic nature of his crime, he was given the death penalty. As he sat on Death Row, the warden unlocked his cell and asked for any requests for his last meal.

"Yes, I would like a silver platter, with a bunch of bananas on it."

The warden shrugged - it wasn't the strangest request he'd ever received. Sure enough, he brought the bunch of bananas, and one by one the world-famous musician ate them all. His meal finished, the warden led him to the electric chair and strapped him in. With a jolt, the lights dimmed slightly, and the band leader lay limp in his chair.

As the warden began to unstrap the unlucky man, he felt a twitch. Suddenly, his eyes opened. He had survived! The warden had no choice but to let him free, since this was clearly an act of God.

Upon returning home, the conductor ran into his team of representatives. They had heard the news and beat him to his house. Overjoyed that the money train could keep coming, they had arranged a special concert to commemorate the miraculous event that had occurred - but he wouldn't have it; he refused to go onstage again.

After hours of convincing, threatening, and sometimes begging (it was the accountants) his legal team finally convinced him to perform again. The following night, he walked onto the stage, tapped his baton, and produced a hand grenade and tossed it into the horn section.

Quickly arrested, sent to jail, charged, and found guilty. For the second time, he sat on Death Row as the warden opened his cell. The warden asked for any requests for the last meal.

"Yes, I would like two silver platters, with two bunches of bananas on them."

The warden returned a few moments later with the requested fruit. One by one, the musical genius peeled and ate them all. He stood up, ready to go to the chair. For the second time, the warden strapped him in, this time making sure the diodes were located properly and that it was a tight fit. This time, there would be no doubt - the warden pulled the lever not once, but twice. A whiff of ozone filled the air as he began clearing the body from the chair - but at his touch, another twitch, and the dead man came to life again.

Frustrated but, knowing a miracle when he saw one, the warden was forced to let him go again.

This time, the man's publicists and lawyers were waiting for him just outside of the prison. What luck that he had survived again! Surely they could arrange a "Miracle" tour, featuring sacred music or themes of Resurrection! But he would have none of it, insisting that he could never again lead an orchestra as he once did.

The publicists fought and argued with him, trying to convince him to see things their way. Only after one of his lawyers pulled a gun on him did he agree to lead the orchestra for the tour.

Opening night, he walks onto the stage, taps his baton, and then pressed a button in his lapel, setting off bombs hidden under the audience's seats. Out of thousands of attendees, only a few made it out alive.

Of course, a trial was just a formality now. He was quickly arrested, tried, and sentenced to death. The warden had to go buy an extra silver platter when he saw the news- he had a hunch he would be ready for the musician - and sure enough, when the Warden asked for any special requests :

"Yes, I'd like three silver platters with three bunches of bananas."

One by one, the bananas were eaten. As he ate, the warden prepared. He wasn't going to be made a fool of three times. He called up an old buddy who was an electrical engineer, and with some jury-rigging had managed to run the entire prison complex's power supply into the chair. Not taking any chances with this one. He led his unfortunate victim to the chair for the third time, strapping him in carefully. He left the room as the capacitors charged, and from a safe distance, the warden pulled the switch.

The electrical discharge was so intense that it very nearly destroyed the room that the chair was in. The walls shook, the ground shuddered, and the ceiling caved in on top of the once-lauded professional. As the guards and laborers picked through the rubble, they saw a shoe - the body must have been trapped under a large chunk of debris.

As the front-end loader lifted the concrete chunk out of the way, the man sat still in his chair, now tipped on its side. Fully alive and awake, unharmed.

The publicists and lawyers had given up. There was too much blood on their hands, and this was getting ridiculous. People wouldn't even have been willing to come to the concert, seeing as how the last one ended. Of course, the entire story had attracted the press, and as the dusty but intact maestro left the prison for the third time, he was surrounded by a swarm of reporters, all trying to get the big scoop.

One reporter managed to get in close enough to talk to him directly - he activated his audio recorder and had his pen ready for a statement.

"Sir! all of the details about your arrest and subsequent executions has gone viral! But there's one thing that everybody wants to know! How did you survive the electric chair so many times? What's your future career plans? What's with all the bananas you allegedly consumed?!"

The maestro sighed and said,
You are my favorite type of human being. I woke people up I laughed so hard. Thanks!

The bartender replies, "The first person who can make my horse cry without harming him wins the money!"

After talking to you I admitted to my partner that I'd had an emotional affair. They felt better that I was being honest and we said we'd make a go of fixing things.

Sounds great in theory but it wasn't working out. I don't want to sound like I'm blaming them since all this was prompted by my screw up, but they don't seem able to move past things. I was tired of having things from the past constantly dredged up and no progress being made on spending quality find together.

So I broke things off tonight and my SO agreed it's for the best. It makes me really sad because I love them like crazy, but it was clear what was happening. Our relationship has been over for a while and it's just been through my sheer will and refusal to give up that my SO hadn't (justifiably) left me. I'm not willing to waste any more of our time.

We'd already discussed what we'd do if things didn't work out when we were deciding whether to make a go of it after I admitted the affair. Because we have kids and just bought a house, we're still going to live together as coparents. We care about each other and want to remain friends, it's just clear that the romantic side of our relationship is dead and was causing pain when we tried to reanimate it.

Eventually we'll set up a second bedroom and when we're ready to sell the house in a few years, we'll probably look for a duplex or property with a guest cottage. Once our households are divided we'll tell people, but we plan on keeping it quiet for now. Our number one priority is making sure the kids can be around both of us full time with our second being that we remain good friends. Both agree the love is still there, it's just not that kind of love anymore (well, at least on their end). :'-(

All in all, I'm really unhappy but think it'll be for the best. My SO deserves to be able to move on and find someone they can trust. I think I'll be happier not being resented and working so hard at a hopeless task. I think the kids will be happier seeing their parents feeling better (particularly my SO, who had suffered a lot from this).

I don't know what the future holds for me when it comes to relationships. I don't think I'm very well suited to romance and monogamy. It was never anything I wanted until meeting my SO. I think for a long while I'll just be on my own and get to know what I'm like as my own person. I've been in this relationship my whole adult life and it's greatly shaped and defined who I am.

Any tips on how to handle things would be greatly appreciated. I'm really bummed right now. I'd also really urge anyone reading this to always be faithful to your SO. It causes a lot of pain and can ruin something really nice.

I'd be more worried about Influenza than MERS or similar things. However, there are a couple of things...

We'll probably never have another Flu epidemic in this world, because most of us have already been exposed to a flu virus in some way, through either vaccination or getting it themselves. The reason the first epidemic happened was because the world was still quite isolated. International travel was not as prolific, so exposure to usually non lethal disease to gain basic immunity was rare. Those who treated those patients with the Spanish flu were often asked before if they had previously had influenza, and were allowed to treat the sick if they had. They might still catch it, but they wouldn't die.

Things like bird flu, which has come around a few times now, really only affects those who are already immunocompromised. This doesn't mean we should ignore the threat, but we should be wary of scare tactics. Sure, it can jump from species to species, but there are ways we can prevent this, through proper farming techniques, quarantines, and vaccinations. If you can get a flu vaccination, do. It really does help prevent spread and protect those who can't protect themselves.
